caption: Jesus directly quotes Psalm 22’s opening from the cross, and Matthew builds more of the scene around it. Clear application does not by itself prove advance prediction.

slides.alt_text: Editorial slide: Did Psalm 22 predict Jesus’s cry? Jesus cries, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”—the opening of Psalm 22.
slides.body: Jesus cries, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”—the opening of Psalm 22.
slides.heading: Did Psalm 22 predict Jesus’s cry?

slides.alt_text: The BSB text of Ps 22:1: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?

slides.heading: Ps 22:1

slides.alt_text: The claimed New Testament fulfilment in Matt 27:46, BSB: About the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
slides.body: About the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
slides.heading: Claimed fulfilment · Matt 27:46

slides.alt_text: Editorial slide: The connection is undeniable Matthew surrounds the cross with more language from the same psalm. Jesus is deliberately portrayed through it.

slides.heading: The connection is undeniable

slides.alt_text: Editorial slide: But quotation is not prediction Psalm 22 is an existing sufferer’s prayer. It never says a future Messiah will repeat these words.

title: My God, why have You forsaken me?
